sources.title: Propositional Logic (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.locator: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-propositional/ (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, first published 2023-05-18, retrieved 2026-11-01)
sources.excerpt: Propositional logic is the study of the meanings of, and the inferential relationships that hold among, sentences based on the role that a specific class of logical operators called the propositional connectives have in determining those sentences' truth or assertability conditions. A is a classical propositional consequence of B if on no assignment of values to the atoms that occur in A and B on which B evaluates as T does A evaluate as F. Classical propositional logic is readily seen to be decidable: Given an arbitrary formula, simply enumerate in the tabular method used above each of the possible sequences of truth values that can be input to its atomic propositional variables, and compute the composition of functions on each of these inputs.

sources.title: Modus ponens (encyclopedia entry)
sources.excerpt: In propositional logic, modus ponens, also known as modus ponendo ponens, conditional elimination, implication elimination, or affirming the antecedent, is a deductive argument form and rule of inference. It can be summarized as "P implies Q. P is true. Therefore, Q must also be true." This argument is valid, but this has no bearing on whether any of the statements in the argument are actually true; for modus ponens to be a sound argument, the premises must be true for any true instances of the conclusion. An argument can be valid but nonetheless unsound if one or more premises are false Given two variables p and q that can either be true or false, implication (p -> q) is defined as all cases being true except where p is true and q is false.

concepts.name: Propositional logic
concepts.definition: The study of the connectives that bind sentences, and of the inferential relationships among the sentences they form.

concepts.name: Propositional variable
concepts.definition: An atomic formula standing for a proposition, with no internal structure.

concepts.name: Propositional connective
concepts.definition: A particle that binds sentences into a new compound sentence of the same evaluation class.

concepts.name: Validity
concepts.definition: The property of a formula that holds on every assignment of truth values.

concepts.name: Satisfiability
concepts.definition: The property of a formula that holds on at least one assignment of truth values.

concepts.name: Consequence
concepts.definition: The relation between formulas in which the consequence holds on every assignment on which the premises hold.

concepts.name: Equivalence
concepts.definition: The relation between formulas that hold on precisely the same assignments.

concepts.name: Modus ponens
concepts.definition: The rule of inference from a conditional and its antecedent to its consequent.

concepts.name: Modus tollens
concepts.definition: The rule of inference from a conditional and the falsity of its consequent to the falsity of its antecedent.

concepts.name: Material conditional
concepts.definition: The classical connective written as p implies q, false in exactly one case.

concepts.name: Truth table
concepts.definition: The table that assigns every combination of truth values to a formula's variables and computes the formula on each.

representations.statement: Propositional logic studies whole sentences and the connectives that join them, such as and, or, not and if-then. It asks when one such sentence follows from others.
assumptions: Whole sentences are the unit of analysis.
includedFacts: The truth table is introduced only at the intermediate level.

representations.audience: a learner who can read a formula
representations.statement: Propositional logic evaluates formulas by assigning truth values to their atomic variables. A formula is valid when it is true on every assignment, satisfiable when it is true on at least one, and a consequence of another when it is true wherever the other is.
includedFacts: Quantified logic, and the non-classical systems.
omitted: Classical two-valued logic only; the material conditional is assumed.

representations.statement: Deciding a formula is mechanical: enumerate every assignment of truth values to the atomic variables, evaluate the formula on each assignment, and read off validity, satisfiability or consequence. The enumeration is finite, and it is what makes the calculus decidable.
includedFacts: The cost of the enumeration grows exponentially in the number of variables.
omitted: Exhaustive enumeration is only affordable for a small number of variables.

representations.statement: Modus ponens: if p implies q, and p is true, then q is true. It is the rule of detachment, and it is how a conditional is cashed in.
assumptions: The conditional is the material conditional.
includedFacts: The soundness of the premises is a separate matter.
omitted: Applies to the material conditional of classical logic.

representations.statement: To apply modus ponens: write the conditional, write the antecedent, and the consequent follows. A modus ponens argument is valid whatever the truth of its premises; it is sound only when the premises are true as well.
assumptions: The two premises are in the same assignment.
includedFacts: The proof-theoretic treatment of Frege's system.
omitted: Validity and soundness are reported separately.

representations.statement: A formula is valid when it is true under every assignment of truth values to its variables. The law of the excluded middle, that p or not p, is valid.
omitted: Validity is about the formula, not about the world.

representations.statement: To test validity, enumerate the assignments and evaluate the formula on each. If it is true on all of them, the formula is valid; if it is true on some, it is satisfiable; if it is false on some assignment on which the premises are all true, it does not follow.
omitted: Only finite formulas over finitely many variables.

representations.statement: A follows from B when every assignment on which B is true also makes A true. Following is about the relation between formulas, not about what happens to be the case.
omitted: A consequence relation is not a causal relation.

prerequisites.note: The connectives act on propositions, so the variable comes first.
Validity is a property of a formula built from the connectives.
Consequence is defined through truth on the assignments.
The material conditional is one of the connectives.
Modus ponens is stated over the material conditional.
The table enumerates the assignments to the variables.
